question.text: Government securities (G-Secs) are considered to have virtually zero credit risk because:

answer.text: They are traded on stock exchanges with high liquidity
They offer the highest returns among all fixed-income instruments
The government is considered unlikely to default on its own borrowings
They are insured by the Deposit Insurance Corporation

explanation.text: The Logic: The workbook says government bonds are the safest for investors, that gilts have no credit risk because the government is considered unlikely to default on its own borrowings, and that government securities do not carry credit risk. T-bills, which are short-term government securities, are also used as a measure of the risk-free rate. These statements directly support the keyed option. The Trap: Option A confuses tradability and liquidity with creditworthiness; an asset can trade frequently without being credit-risk free. Option B is incorrect because higher returns are typically associated with higher risk, not the absence of credit risk, and G-Secs are not the highest-yielding fixed-income instruments. Option D refers to deposit insurance, which applies to certain bank deposits and not to government securities, so it does not explain why G-Secs are treated as free of credit risk. Note: The workbook's reason for treating G-Secs as effectively free of credit risk is the assumption that the issuer (the government) will not default on its own borrowings, which is why T-bill yields are used as a benchmark risk-free return.
